explanation_box.text: This reptile is small and agile, and thus able to climb up to safe places to deposit eggs. He is quick and able to avoid and/or get away from predators. Also, the stripes on his back are useful in attracting a mate. This is why he achieved a pretty decent score.

This is the same reptile from the previous slide. His fertility score went down because he is much quicker and more agile in warmer weather. This study took place in cooler temperatures, so he is not as fast, or as able to climb to the same heights as previously.

This creature (whose name is "Green Gigliotti") is continuing to receive lower fertility scores, and in this case, there are two main reasons.  In this study, the temperature is cooler, so again, he is not functioning at top speed or agility.  But also, the availability of mates is greatly decreased since the last study.

So, the Green Gigliotti has gone full circle, through one full year, and we are back where we started in the first study. We've got warmer temperatures, and he is operating at peak capacity, once again achieving a "7", which is not bad.

It is not often that a reptile species achieves a fertility score of 10, but in this case, here is what happened with the Green Gigliotti...   The researchers recording the data became sort of enchanted by this particular species, and they began to subconsciously root for him to achieve higher scores each time.  They counted offspring that were technically dead, or close to dead, as surviving. Their bias eventually resulted in this inaccurate score.

So - when the researchers over-counted in the last study, resulting in a "10" - the mistake was not discovered in time for the next count - resulting in a second inaccurate score of 10. Now that the error has been revealed and discussed, this abberration should not occur going forward.

So, a number of things contributed to this dip. The time of year is now cooler weather once again, which has the effect of lowering the score in general.. But also, the researchers - being told of their mistake - overcompensated while trying to correct it and went way too low.

This super low score is an extension, a continuation, if you will, of the "2" that we observed in the previous study.  With warmer weather coming, and more accurate counting - we should start to see the numbers get back to "normal" soon...
So - since the last study - a certain species of raccoon literally invaded the area where the study was taking place, devouring nearly all of the eggs that were attempting to hatch.

After the issue with the raccoon infestation, the Green Gigliotti adapted and started depositing its eggs into small crevices/openings in trees, where the predators could not access.  This number is still high, and is expected to drop soon.
With normal temperatures, and other variables now under control, the score is now settling back into its average, expected range.
Again, we are now cruising in the usual, expected range of fertility for a Green Gigliotti.
So, it appears the raccoons adapted and figured out a way to get to the eggs. This has been an unfortunate setback for the GG reptile.

The Green Giggy (as it has now become affectionately known) has once again figured out a way to evade the troublesome raccoons. It developed an annoying chemical "spray" that is sprayed around the eggs, which the raccoons do NOT like.. so our number has returned to its usual baseline.
It seems the new "spray" technique is very effective, and many offspring are now surviving. THis is good news for Green Giggy fans everywhere.
We are now operating at the usual baseline. The expected score now is around 6 to 8.
